title: Practice: inscribed polygons
intro: Nine questions. Have compasses and a ruler nearby — trying the constructions on paper makes these much easier.

questions.prompt: Put the steps for constructing an inscribed regular hexagon in order.

items.text: Draw a circle and keep the compasses set to its radius
Mark an arc on the circumference and label it A
With the point on A, mark the next arc along and label it B
Repeat to mark C, D, E and F
Join A to B, B to C, … and F back to A

hints: You cannot step round the circle until the compasses are set to the radius.
questions.explanation: Setting the compasses to the radius first is the key step, because every side of a regular hexagon is exactly one radius long.

questions.prompt: Each side of a regular hexagon inscribed in a circle is the same length as the circle's radius.
hints: The hexagon splits into six triangles meeting at the centre. What kind of triangles?
questions.explanation: True. The angle at the centre of each triangle is $360^\circ \div 6 = 60^\circ$, and two of its sides are radii, so all three angles are $60^\circ$. The triangles are equilateral, so the hexagon side equals the radius.

questions.prompt: The side of an inscribed regular hexagon is equal to one part of this circle. Click that part.
hints: It runs from the centre to the circumference.
questions.explanation: The **radius**. That is why you keep the compasses set to the radius when you step round the circle to make a hexagon.

questions.prompt: Complete the angle at the centre for each regular polygon.
Use the explorer to find the regular polygon whose angle at the centre is $40^\circ$.
questions.explanation: $360 \div 40 = 9$, so it is a regular **nonagon** (9 sides).

questions.prompt: You have constructed the six points of an inscribed hexagon, A to F. How do you get an inscribed **equilateral triangle**?

options.text: Join every other point: A to C, C to E, E to A
Bisect each side of the hexagon

hints: An equilateral triangle needs its three vertices spaced evenly round the circle.
questions.explanation: Joining every other point gives three vertices $120^\circ$ apart at the centre, which is an equilateral triangle. A, B and C are bunched together on one side.

questions.prompt: Starting from an inscribed square, what do you construct to get a regular **octagon**?

options.text: The perpendicular bisectors of two neighbouring sides of the square
An angle of $60^\circ$ at each vertex

hints: You need four new points exactly halfway between the square's vertices.
questions.explanation: The perpendicular bisector of a side of the square passes through the centre and cuts the circle halfway between two vertices. Bisecting AY and AX gives the four new points, making eight equally spaced vertices.

questions.prompt: A square is inscribed in a circle of radius 10 cm. Its diagonals are diameters. Find the area of the square.
hints: Split the square into 4 right-angled triangles with legs of 10 cm, or use Pythagoras to find the side.
questions.explanation: The square splits into four triangles each with base and height 10 cm: $4 \times \frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 10 = 200\ \text{cm}^2$. (Or: side$^2 = 10^2 + 10^2 = 200$.)

questions.prompt: Which of these are you allowed to use when a question says **construct**?

options.text: A ruler, for drawing straight lines

hints: Constructions are exact because nothing is measured.
questions.explanation: Compasses, a straight edge and a pencil only. Measuring with a ruler or a protractor would introduce the errors that constructions are designed to avoid.
